en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Section on the Indivisible, from the Chapter of Puzzles (Meṇḍakapañha)
3. The Question on Fear and Fearlessness Regarding Death “Venerable Nāgasena, this was said by the Blessed One:
‘All tremble at punishment; all fear death. Yet, it has also been said:”
‘The Arahant has transcended all fear.

Now, venerable Nāgasena, does the Arahant tremble at the fear of punishment? Or do the beings in hell tremble at death as they are burning, boiling, heated, and inflamed, falling away from that great hell with its network of blazing flames?
If, venerable Nāgasena, it was said by the Blessed One—
“If it is true that ‘all tremble at punishment, all fear death,’ then the statement that ‘the Arahant has transcended all fear’ must be false. Conversely,
if it was spoken by the Blessed One that ‘the Arahant has transcended all fear,’ then the statement that ‘all tremble at punishment, all fear death’ must also be false.”
“This is a dilemma with two sides that has come to you; it must be resolved by you.
“Great King, this statement was not spoken by the Blessed One with reference to the Arahants:
‘All tremble at punishment; all fear death.’”
The Arahant is set apart from that matter; the cause of fear has been removed for the Arahant.
Great King, it was with reference to those beings who possess defilements, who have an excessive view of self, and who are elated or dejected by pleasure and pain, that the Blessed One said:
“All tremble at punishment; all fear death.”
Great King, for the Arahant all destinations have been cut off, the womb has been destroyed, rebirth-linking has been impaired, the rafters are broken,
all attachments to existence have been uprooted, all conditioned formations have been severed, the wholesome and unwholesome have been slain, ignorance has been dispelled,
consciousness rendered seedless, all defilements burnt away, and the worldly conditions have been transcended; therefore—
The Arahant does not tremble at any fears.
In this regard, Great King, suppose a king had four chief ministers who were protectors, possessed of renown, trustworthy, and established in positions of great authority.
Then, when some royal business arose, the king might issue a command to all the people throughout his own realm: "Let everyone pay me tribute; you four chief ministers, accomplish that task for me."
“Would fear and terror arise, Great King, in those four chief ministers because of the fear of the army?
“No, venerable sir.
“For what reason, Great King?”

“Venerable sir, they have been placed by the king in the highest position; they owe him no tribute, for they have transcended the power [of debt]. It was with reference to the remainder that the king commanded: ‘Let all of them pay me tribute.
“In the same way, great king, these words were not spoken by the Blessed One with reference to the Arahants.
The Arahant has been excluded from that matter; the cause of fear has been removed for the Arahant. As for those beings, great king, who still possess defilements...”
“With reference to those who have an excessive view of self and those who are elated by pleasure and dejected by pain, the Blessed One said:
‘All tremble at punishment; all fear death.
Therefore, the Arahant does not tremble at any fears.”
“Venerable Nāgasena, this statement is not incomplete; it is a complete statement when it says ‘all.
Therefore, give me a further reason to establish that statement.

“In this case, Great King, suppose the headman of a village were to command his messenger: ‘Come, messenger, gather all the villagers in this village together quickly and bring them into my presence.’”

Saying, “Very well, master,” and having accepted the command, he would stand in the middle of the village and proclaim three times: “All those who are villagers in this village, let them all assemble very quickly in the presence of the master!
Then, at the word of the commander, those villagers would assemble in great haste and report to the master of the village: “Master, all the villagers have assembled; do whatever you must do.
In this way, Great King, that master of the village, while assembling his men in the hamlet, commands all the villagers, and they—
Not all those who were commanded assemble; only the householders assemble.
Even if the village headman accepts [the report], thinking, "I have only this many villagers," yet other people—more numerous than those accounted—have not arrived:

women, men, female and male slaves, laborers, servants, villagers, the sick, cattle, buffaloes, goats, sheep, and dogs. All those who have not arrived are uncounted; [he counts] only the householders.
“Because [the command] was issued by taking [others] as a basis, saying, ‘Let everyone assemble.
In the same way, Great King, this statement was not spoken by the Blessed One with reference to the Arahants;
the Arahant is excluded from that matter, for the cause of fear has been removed for the Arahant. Those beings, Great King, who possess defilements—”
And regarding those who have an excessive view of self, and those who are puffed up by pleasure or dejected by pain—it was with reference to them that the Blessed One said:
“All tremble at punishment; all fear death.
Therefore, the Arahant does not tremble at any fears.

"There is, Great King, a statement with a remainder [of meaning] and a meaning with a remainder; there is a statement with a remainder and a meaning without remainder; there is a statement without remainder and a meaning with a remainder; and there is a statement without remainder and a meaning without remainder.

The meaning should be accepted according to each of these cases. Great King, the meaning should be accepted by means of five reasons: by the direct word (*āhacca-pada*), by the flavor (*rasa*), by the lineage of teachers (*ācariya-vaṃsa*), by the intention (*adhippāya*), and by the superiority of the reason (*kāraṇuttariyatā*)."
For here, "the word of direct impact" (*āhacca-pada*) refers to the Sutta; "the flavor" (*rasa*) refers to that which is in conformity with the Sutta;
and "the lineage of teachers" (*ācariya-vaṃsa*) refers to the doctrine of the teachers.
"Intention" means one's own opinion.
"Superiority of reason" means a reason that is consistent with these four.
"Great King, it is by these five reasons that a matter should be accepted."
“Thus this question is well-determined.
“Let it be so, venerable Nāgasena; I accept it as such.
Let the Arahant be set aside in that matter; let the rest of beings tremble, but as for those in hell, they are destined for hell.”
Beings experiencing intense, sharp, and bitter sensations, with all their limbs and members burning and blazing, their mouths crying out in piteous weeping, lamentation, and wailing;

overcome by unbearable and piercing suffering, without protection, without refuge, and having become homeless; afflicted by constant grief, destined for their final and last state, devoted solely to sorrow;
possessing heat, sharpness, fierceness, harshness, and scorching brilliance, they produce a great sound of terrifying and fear-inducing cries.
“Are they crowded with a garland of sixfold entangling nets, spreading their blazing speed for a hundred yojanas in every direction,
falling from the Kadariya and Tapana great hells, and terrified of Death?
“Yes, Great King,” he replied.
“But, venerable Nāgasena, hell is a place where only painful feelings are experienced; why then do those beings in hell, when passing away from that hell which is exclusively painful, fear death?
Why do they take delight in hell? “Great King, those beings in hell do not take delight in hell; they only desire to be released from it.
Great King, it is the power of death itself by which that terror arises in them.”
“Venerable Nāgasena, I do not believe this, that terror arises in those who desire to be released at the moment of death.
Venerable Nāgasena, that situation is laughable—that they should obtain what they have longed for! Convince me by means of a reason.
“Death, great king, is a terrifying matter for those who have not seen the Truth; herein people tremble and are struck with fear.”
And whoever, O Great King, fears the black snake, he fears the black snake while fearing death.
And whoever fears the elephant … the lion … the tiger … the leopard … the bear … the hyena … the buffalo … the gayal … fire … water … a stump … or a thorn, [he fears these while fearing death].
And whoever fears the spear, he fears the spear because he fears death.
For death itself, O Great King, has the power of its own inherent nature; by that power of its own inherent nature, beings with defilements tremble and fear death.
Even those beings in hell, O Great King, though they desire to be released, tremble and fear death.
"In this case, Great King, a fatty tumor might arise on a man's body.
Afflicted by that disease and desiring to be freed from the calamity, he would summon a physician, a surgeon.
Having accepted his request, that physician, the surgeon, would prepare the instruments for the extraction of that disease."
“Suppose one were to prepare a lancet, sharpen it, place two salākā sticks into a fire,
and grind caustic salt on a whetstone. Would fear arise, Great King, in that patient from the cutting with the sharp lancet,
the burning of the two salākā sticks, and the application of the caustic salt?”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“In this way, great king, even for that sick man who desires to be freed from his disease, terror arises out of fear of the pain.
In the same way, great king, even for the beings in hell who desire to be freed from hell, terror arises out of fear of death.”

“Suppose, great king, a man had committed an offense against his lord and was bound with shackles, cast into a dungeon, and desiring to be released. His lord, wishing to release him, were to summon him.
Would fear arise in that man who had offended his lord, great king, upon seeing his lord, knowing: ‘I am one who has committed an offense’?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Thus, Great King, even for that man who has offended his lord and desires to be released, terror arises out of fear of his lord.
In the same way, Great King, even for the beings in hell who desire to be released from hell, terror arises out of fear of death.
“Furthermore, venerable sir, tell me another reason by which I might gain conviction.”
“Suppose, great king, a man were bitten by a venomous snake with fangs;
he would fall down because of that effect of the poison, or leap up, or roll about, or writhe.
Then another man, having brought that very same venomous snake with its fangs using a powerful mantra-word, would make him drink back that same venom from his bite. What do you think, great king?”
“Would fear arise in that man who has been poisoned when the snake whose venom he was bitten by approaches for the sake of his safety?”—
“Yes, venerable sir.”—
“In this way, great king, even when such a snake approaches for the sake of his safety, fear arises in him.”
"In the same way, Great King, terror arises even for beings in hell who desire to be released from hell because of the fear of death.
Death, Great King, is undesirable to all beings; therefore, beings in hell, though desiring to be completely freed from hell, are afraid of death.
"Excellent, venerable Nāgasena! It is so; thus do I accept it."
The third question: On the fear and lack of fear of death.
